Admitting Officer

Emergency Department

Newtown Hospital

13/09/2014

Dear Sir,

Re Ms. Sally McConville,

38 years of age

Comment [teacher1]: repeated in Introduction

I am writing to refer Ms. McConville, a 38-year-old administrator, whose symptoms and signs
are suggestive of acute asthma. She needs your urgent intervention.

The patient is a non-smoker. Unfortunately, she has been suffering from asthma, for which
she takes ramipril, paroxetine, fluticose and ventoline.

On 10/09/2014, the patient came complaining of symptoms related to a viral upper
respiratory tract infection, including a runny nose, productive cough and fever. However, her
examination was unremarkable. Hence, the patient was instructed to continue taking
ventoline, and she was given a certified work leave. Unlikely, 2 days later, the conditioned
was not improved, as she reported that she had experienced a difficulty in breathing and
fever. On examination, there were wheezes over the chest and increasing the work of breath,
though there were no cripitations. The patient was diagnosed with an infective exacerbation
of asthma, so that amoxicillin and prednisolone were prescribed .

Today, the condition has been detoriated because the patient presented with exaggerated
chest tightness. Moreover, there where genralized wheeze, bibasal lung crepitations, a high
respiratory rate and an obvious depedndence on the accessory muscle. Thus, salbuatmol was
prescribed, but there was no improvement.

In light of the above, the patient is being referred for further management and investigations
because of the possibility of pneumonia. Should you have any queries, please do not hesitate
to contact me.
